title: Approximating the Euclidean Ball by Polytopes:Surprising Rates in High Dimensions

paper.title: Approximating the Euclidean Ball by Polytopes: Surprising Rates in High Dimensions
paper.abstract:
Abstract We determine the sharp dependence on the dimension in the asymptotic
approximation of the Euclidean unit ball B 2 d ⊂ ℝ d B_{2}^{d}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} by
polytopes with a prescribed number of vertices in the (relative) symmetric
difference metric. Specifically, we prove that lim N → ∞ N 2 d − 1 inf P ∈ 𝒫 d ​ ( N ) vol d ⁡ ( P ​ △ ​ B 2 d ) vol d ⁡ ( B 2 d ) = Θ ( d − 1 / 2 ) , \lim_{N\to\infty}N^{\frac{2}{d-1}}\inf_{P\in\mathcal{P}_{d}(N)}\frac{\vol_{d}(P\triangle B_{2}^{d})}{\vol_{d}(B_{2}^{d})}=\Theta(d^{-1/2}), where 𝒫 d ​ ( N ) \mathcal{P}_{d}(N) denotes the class of polytopes in ℝ d \mathbb{R}^{d} with at most N N vertices, with no containment restriction.
Equivalently, the classical Laguerre–Delone triangulation numbers
satisfy ldel d − 1 = Θ ( d − 1 / 2 ) \ldel_{d-1}=\Theta(d^{-1/2}) .
This improves the lower bound Ω ⁡ ( d − 1 ) \Omega(d^{-1}) of Böröczky (2000) and the upper bound O ⁡ ( 1 ) O(1) of Ludwig et al. (2006) .
The result contrasts with approximation by polytopes with a prescribed
number of facets, for which the corresponding asymptotic coefficient
has order one ( Kur, 2020 ) . We also establish non-asymptotic approximation bounds showing that,
for every fixed ε ∈ ( 0 , 1 ) \varepsilon\in(0,1) , the ball admits an ε \varepsilon -approximation by a polytope with at most exp ⁡ ( C ⁡ ( ε ) ​ d ) \exp(C(\varepsilon)\sqrt{d}) vertices.
In contrast, we prove that approximating the hypercube to any fixed ε \varepsilon -accuracy requires at least exp ⁡ ( c ⁡ ( ε ) ​ d ) \exp(c(\varepsilon)d) vertices. Consequently, the Euclidean ball does not maximize the optimal
relative approximation error among convex bodies, even up to an
absolute multiplicative constant at the same vertex budget.
Thus Macbeath’s theorem ( Macbeath, 1951 ) , which establishes the
extremality of the ball for approximation by inscribed polytopes,
does not extend to polytopes in arbitrary position.

sections.heading: Sharp dimensional order for vertex approximation.
sections.text: In Theorem 1 , we prove that ℰ d = Θ ( d − 1 / 2 ) , ldel d − 1 = Θ ( d − 1 / 2 ) , \mathcal{E}_{d}=\Theta(d^{-1/2}),\qquad\ldel_{d-1}=\Theta(d^{-1/2}), with upper and lower leading constants differing by a factor of two. This improves both previously known bounds by a factor of d \sqrt{d} . Consequently, an unrestricted vertex budget gives a smaller asymptotic error than an equal facet budget by a factor of order d \sqrt{d} , while removing the inscribed restriction improves the vertex coefficient by a factor of order d 3 / 2 d^{3/2} . A deterministic dilation of a random inscribed polytope attains the optimal error up to an absolute constant. The next result helps explain this surprising vertex–facet separation through the effect of facet geometry.

sections.heading: The cost of simplicial facets.
sections.text: In Theorem 2 , we prove that ldiv d − 1 s ¯ = Θ ⁡ ( d ) , ldiv d − 1 s ¯ = Θ ⁡ ( d ) . \underline{\ldiv^{s}_{d-1}}=\Theta(\sqrt{d}),\qquad\overline{\ldiv^{s}_{d-1}}=\Theta(\sqrt{d}). Thus requiring all facets to be simplices worsens the optimal facet-constrained coefficient by a factor of order d \sqrt{d} . The upper bound uses the same random construction as the vertex theorem, together with the expected-facet-count asymptotics of Buchta et al. (1985) ; Buchta (1987) .

sections.heading: Failure of the ball’s extremality without containment.
sections.text: The preceding comparison rules out an unrestricted vertex analogue of Macbeath’s extremality theorem ( Macbeath, 1951 ) ; see ( 13 ) below. Even allowing an absolute multiplicative constant, the ball does not bound the optimal relative error of every convex body at the same vertex budget. The same exponential obstruction holds for a single sequence of convex bodies with real-analytic boundaries and everywhere positive Gaussian curvature. Further applications concern smooth convex bodies, surface area deviation, and restrictions on the number of k k -faces; see Corollaries 1 , 6 and 7 . We next give the background for these comparisons before stating the main results precisely.

sections.heading: 4 Discussion
sections.text: In Banach–Mazur distance, polar duality keeps vertex and facet budgets comparable for origin-symmetric bodies. In the symmetric difference metric, inscribed and circumscribed approximation errors are also known to be very close (see Section 1 ). In contrast, in the unrestricted case our results show that a vertex construction significantly outperforms its facet counterpart both in the asymptotic coefficient and in the finite regime. Here we provide some additional context and intuition for this rather surprising discrepancy, with a focus on the non-asymptotic perspective of Theorem 4 . P=R^{-1}K,\qquad R^{d}\vol_{d}(B_{2}^{d})=\mathbb{E}\vol_{d}(K). Assume a fixed target accuracy 0 < ε < 1 0<\varepsilon<1 throughout. sections.heading: Large facet count.
sections.text: We can get an initial idea by looking at the combinatorial complexity of the random polytope beyond its vertex definition. It is simplest to analyze its number of facets. The exact expected count can be obtained by summing an indicator variable over all candidate simplices. For the convex hull P ~ N \widetilde{P}_{N} of N N independent uniform points on 𝕊 d − 1 \mathbb{S}^{d-1} , Bonnet and O’Reilly (2022, Theorem 4.3) show, when d = o ⁡ ( N ) d=o(N) and log ⁡ N = o ⁡ ( d ) \log N=o(d) , that 𝔼 ​ f d − 1 ​ ( P ~ N ) = [ ( 4 ​ π + o ⁡ ( 1 ) ) ​ log ⁡ ( N / d ) ] ( d − 1 ) / 2 . \mathbb{E}f_{d-1}(\widetilde{P}_{N})=\bigl[(4\pi+o(1))\log(N/d)\bigr]^{(d-1)/2}. Our construction uses antipodal pairs, so this theorem does not apply directly. The corresponding candidate-facet calculation requires avoidance of two antipodal caps, but gives the same leading logarithmic order. At the scale log ⁡ N = Θ ε ​ ( d ) \log N=\Theta_{\varepsilon}(\sqrt{d}) dictated by Theorem 4 , log ⁡ 𝔼 ​ f d − 1 ​ ( P ) = d 4 ​ log ⁡ d + Θ ε ​ ( d ) . \log\mathbb{E}f_{d-1}(P)=\frac{d}{4}\log d+\Theta_{\varepsilon}(d). Although the vertex budget is sub-exponential, the expected number of facets is super-exponential. Theorem 2 provides an independent perspective on this large facet count. It shows that approximation with a prescribed number of simplicial facets suffers an additional d \sqrt{d} penalty asymptotically, compared to the unrestricted facet problem. The facet-count estimate describes the present construction as d d grows, while Theorem 2 first takes the facet budget to infinity in each fixed dimension.

sections.heading: 6.2 Open problems
sections.text: Open Problem 1 (Are random constructions asymptotically optimal?) . A constant-factor gap remains between the best known upper and lower bounds in both the facet and vertex problems. In the facet case, Hoehner and Kur (2021) connected the optimality of random polytopes to the geometric balls and bins problem, which concerns the optimality of random partial coverings of the sphere (see also Hoehner and Kur (2026) and Hoehner and Thäle (2026) ). Motivated by this connection, we conjecture that the random construction with an optimally chosen common facet height is asymptotically optimal: its expected symmetric volume difference, divided by the smallest possible symmetric volume difference among polytopes with the same number of facets, tends to one as M → ∞ M\to\infty followed by d → ∞ d\to\infty . In the vertex case, it remains unclear whether the random construction achieves the optimal leading constant, even after optimizing the common sampling radius. The last-named author suspects that it is suboptimal. Indeed, the additional factor d − 1 / 2 d^{-1/2} established here arises from fluctuations of the local approximation error, suggesting that the leading constant may be sensitive to the arrangement of the vertices. A more regular configuration could conceivably reduce these fluctuations and improve upon independent uniform sampling. Open Problem 2 . Comparing Theorem 7 and ( 49 ) in their common range of applicability, we see that there is a gap of order d \sqrt{d} between these lower bounds. An interesting open question is then: What is the best possible constant c ⁡ ( d , k ) c(d,k) so that for a sequence of best-approximating polytopes P M ∈ 𝒫 d , k ​ ( M ) P_{M}\in\mathcal{P}_{d,k}(M) in arbitrary position, we have vol d ⁡ ( B 2 d ​ △ ​ P M ) = Θ ⁡ ( c ⁡ ( d , k ) ) ​ M − 2 d − 1 ​ ? \vol_{d}(B_{2}^{d}\triangle P_{M})=\Theta(c(d,k))M^{-\frac{2}{d-1}}\,? In the endpoint cases k = 0 k=0 and k = d − 1 k=d-1 , upper estimates with the sharp dimensional order have been obtained by using random polytopes, as can be seen from comparing the results in this paper and Kur (2020) ; Ludwig et al. (2006) . sections.text: This proof uses the local version of the approximation problem. For the vertex formulation that we consider, the general construction is an affine interpolator with up to N N vertices chosen to lie on the graph of a convex function (a quadratic is a standard choice). In the unrestricted case, the last coordinate of the nodes is allowed to move. Our lower bound works by precisely estimating the approximation error on each simplex of the Delaunay triangulation. Locally, arbitrary shifts in the vertex heights amount to adding some affine function to the error. We construct one bounded sign whose average against every affine function is zero, but whose average against the positive quadratic gap remains a fixed fraction of that gap. The resulting inequality can then be summed over the triangulation.
